concept.name: HTTP/2 Connection Multiplexing

relationships.description: Connects HTTP/2 Connection Multiplexing to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

concept.tagline: Multiplexing concurrent binary streams over a single TCP connection with HPACK header compression and flow control, eliminating HTTP/1.1 HoL blocking.
concept.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of HTTP/2—from binary frame streams and HPACK dynamic tables to TCP-level head-of-line blocking, L4 pinning, and CVE-2023-44487 Rapid Reset.

spark.summary: HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) multiplexes concurrent binary request/response streams over a single TCP connection using HPACK header compression and flow control, eliminating HTTP/1.1 application-layer head-of-line blocking.
spark.keyTakeaway: HTTP/2 removes the 6-connection-per-origin browser limit and HTTP/1.1 pipelining stalls, but all streams still share one TCP congestion window—so packet loss above ~1–2% causes TCP-level head-of-line blocking that only HTTP/3 (QUIC) solves.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** HTTP/1.1 forces browsers to open 6 parallel TCP connections per origin (each paying TCP + TLS handshakes and cold slow-start) and still stalls behind slow responses.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Interleaved HTTP/2 Frames on 1 TCP Connection (vs. TCP Packet Loss) (Client (1 TCP) -> TCP Congestion Win -> Origin / Envoy); Mobile HTTP/3 (QUIC) -> Edge CDN -> Internal HTTP/2 L7 Envoy Mesh (Mobile Client -> Edge CDN / ALB -> Envoy L7 Mesh -> Backend Pods).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Compare the three HTTP generations across multiplexing, HoL blocking, and proxy support. Modern platforms terminate **HTTP/3 (QUIC)** and **HTTP/2** at the CDN/edge (protecting mobile users from packet-loss HoL stalls) and route **HTTP/2** internally through **L7.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore how HTTP/2 interacts with L7 load balancing, keep-alive timeouts, and TLS handshake storms.

learningJourney.title: What is HTTP/2 Binary Framing & Multiplexing
learningJourney.explanation:
HTTP/1.1 forces browsers to open 6 parallel TCP connections per origin (each paying TCP + TLS handshakes and cold slow-start) and still stalls behind slow responses. **HTTP/2 (RFC 9113)** splits every message into binary frames (`HEADERS`, `DATA`, `SETTINGS`, `WINDOW_UPDATE`, `RST_STREAM`, `GOAWAY`) tagged with a 31-bit **Stream ID**.

Dozens of concurrent streams (`SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS = 100–256`) interleave on **one** warmed TCP connection, while **HPACK (RFC 7541)** compresses repeated headers/cookies by ~80% using a static table, a 4,096-byte dynamic table, and Huffman coding.

sectionDiagram.title: Interleaved HTTP/2 Frames on 1 TCP Connection (vs. TCP Packet Loss)
sectionDiagram.summary: HTTP/2 eliminates application-layer HoL blocking, but a single dropped TCP packet still stalls all multiplexed streams.

learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how HTTP/2 Binary Framing & Multiplexing works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Why Multiplexing & Connection Coalescing Speed Up Pages & Meshes
learningJourney.explanation: Modern web apps issue 40–150 concurrent requests per origin. Collapsing them onto one warmed TCP connection lets TCP's congestion window grow large, eliminates ephemeral port exhaustion, and cuts TLS handshake storms—especially when wildcard certs enable **connection coalescing** across subdomains.

ideas.title: HPACK Stateful Ordering
ideas.description: Because HPACK's 4 KB dynamic table is stateful per connection, frames must be processed in strict TCP order, and proxies must bound dynamic table memory.

ideas.title: Rapid Reset DoS (CVE-2023-44487)
ideas.description: Attackers can open and immediately `RST_STREAM` millions of streams per second, exhausting backend workers without hitting `MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS`. Patched HTTP/2 stacks rate-limit consecutive resets.

learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Why Multiplexing & Connection Coalescing Speed Up Pages & Meshes under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Where HTTP/2 Wins (and Where HTTP/3 QUIC or L7 Proxies Are Needed)
learningJourney.explanation: HTTP/2 shines on reliable fiber/datacenter links; lossy mobile networks and L4 load balancers expose its TCP coupling.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Broadband CDN & Internal gRPC Meshes
benefits: Zero connection-pool churn, 80% smaller headers via HPACK, and 100+ concurrent RPCs per socket.
costs: Requires L7-aware load balancers (Envoy/ALB/Nginx) to balance per-stream instead of per-connection.

comparison.choice: Prefer HTTP/3 (QUIC): Lossy Cellular Networks (>2% Loss)
benefits: QUIC runs over UDP with independent per-stream recovery, eliminating TCP head-of-line blocking.
costs: Higher UDP CPU overhead and occasional enterprise firewall UDP/443 blocking (fallback to H2).

benefits: L7 proxies demultiplex streams evenly across newly scaled backend pods.
costs: L4 VIPs pin all multiplexed streams on one TCP socket to a single backend pod.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: Tuning Flow-Control Windows, Max Streams & Rapid Reset Caps
learningJourney.explanation: The RFC default `64 KiB` flow-control window throttles high-BDP (bandwidth-delay product) links to a few MB/s. Tune `initial_stream_window_size` (1–4 MB) and `max_concurrent_streams` (100–256) on Envoy/Nginx.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```yaml
# Envoy HTTP/2 upstream/downstream protocol tuning
typed_extension_protocol_options:
  envoy.extensions.upstreams.http.v3.HttpProtocolOptions:
    "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.upstreams.http.v3.HttpProtocolOptions
    explicit_http_config:
      http2_protocol_options:
        max_concurrent_streams: 128
        initial_stream_window_size: 1048576      # 1 MiB per stream (vs 64 KiB default)
        initial_connection_window_size: 16777216 # 16 MiB per connection
```

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: HTTP/1.1 vs. HTTP/2 vs. HTTP/3 (QUIC)
learningJourney.explanation: Compare the three HTTP generations across multiplexing, HoL blocking, and proxy support.

benefits: Works with every L4 load balancer and simple text debugging.
costs: 6-connection browser cap, repeated TLS handshakes, and application-layer HoL blocking.

benefits: Mature L7 proxy support, HPACK header compression, and universal gRPC transport.
costs: TCP-level HoL blocking under packet loss and L4 connection pinning.

benefits: 0-RTT/1-RTT handshakes, connection migration across Wi-Fi/5G, and zero cross-stream HoL blocking.
costs: Higher server CPU per packet than kernel-offloaded TCP.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.explanation: Modern platforms terminate **HTTP/3 (QUIC)** and **HTTP/2** at the CDN/edge (protecting mobile users from packet-loss HoL stalls) and route **HTTP/2** internally through **L7 Envoy sidecars** for per-stream load balancing.

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
